Let me say out loud what I think everyone is feeling right now…

Jensen was the poster child for a CEO who didn’t get caught up in these types of controversies. 

He is the last person you would think could get caught up in something like this.

When it comes to the AI revolution, he is at the center of it. Without NVIDIA, there is no AI revolution. In many respects, he has been emblematic of American capitalism over the past few years. A dishwasher at Denny’s had an idea and turned it into a $5T company. 

Everyone simply thought Jensen was above these types of things. 

I don’t even want this to be about a rich powerful man cheating on his wife…we have heard this story over and over again. That isn’t to normalize it as being okay, but it’s not really shocking. 

However, the broader issue here is what infidelity implies about someone’s character. You can make many excuses to justify it, but we all know that infidelity is not a good thing. There is a lack of morality involved when it comes to cheating.

When you are the CEO of a $5T company, the question now emerges: if you can lie to your wife, can you also lie about other things…like China’s access to your technology?

I don’t really know what to think. My gut tells me that Jensen has acted ethically in most fronts when it comes to business, but I also know that to build a $5T company, the lines around ethics can blur easily. A framework for being able to make sense of and justify your actions is very, very important and we all simply don’t know if this affair will result in anything bad in regards to America’s national security with China.

I don’t think this is good for the stock market or the AI trade. There will now be investigations and concerns around Nvidia and Nvidia is in control of how all the semis do. I also think this story may have leaked last week and that’s part of why we saw such a massive de-risking by institutions. 

I do think there is a world where the market moves beyond this, especially if the investigation doesn’t show any meaningful compromised intelligence. I also think the public will be willing to forgive Jensen, at the end of the day he is a human and infidelity has obviously been part of many marriages, much less such a high profile one. 

This is just a really weird moment and not something I ever expected from Jensen. It will now be up to the market to decide how important and meaningful this is when it comes to where the AI trade goes.

posts.text:
The P in JEPA stands for predictive.
The main distinction is not between JEA and JEPA, but between Joint Embedding (predictive or not) and generative architectures.
Whether a predictor is necessary depends on the task.

Given observations x and y (y being available only during training), a generative architectures predicts y from x. The loss is the divergence between y and its prediction:
  L = divergence(y, pred(enc(x)) )

A JEA encodes y as well and minimizes the divergence between the representations of x and y, while preventing collapse:
  L = divergence( enc(y), enc(x) ) + R( enc(y), enc(x) )
Where R is the anti-collapse regularizer, which may be computed over a batch of samples.
JEA are used when the prediction has no particular direction, i.e. when x and y are different views of the same scene. The idea for JEA is very old. Becker and Hinton proposed a simple model in 1989 where the anticollapse was based on information maximization. Schmidhuber had a version in 1992 based on redundancy minimization. At NIPS 1993, I proposed Siamese nets, which was a contrastive method to train JEA. Such contrastive methods gained popu.arity after Google's SimCLR paper in 2020. In 2021, Stéphane Deny in my group proposed the Barlow Twins redundancy reduction regularizer, which seemed to work at scale. This was shortly followed by VICReg by Adrien Bardes, Jean Ponce, and me, and last year by SIGReg by Randall Balestriero and me. 
DINO is a JEA method that comes from a long string of papers from Piotr Bojanowski's group at FAIR-Paris, starting with Noise as Targets (2017), Deep Clustering (2018-2020), and DINO v1-v3 which are contrastive between clusters, not samples.

JEPA adds a predictor, which is useful when the prediction is non-symetric. For example, when x is a degraded/corrupted version of y, or when x is a present observation and y a future observation (temporal prediction). The loss is:
  L = divergence( enc(y), pred(enc(x)) ) + R( enc(y), enc(x) )

All of these models can be augmented by an action variable a, fed to the predictor, encoding an action, intervention, or transformation to produce y from x.
This turns the system into a "world model". In a JEPA, the loss becomes
  L = divergence( enc(y), pred(enc(x), a) ) + R( enc(y), enc(x) )

My point is about sequencing. The legal rules are the plumbing. Treasury can't overdraft the TGA and the Fed can't buy debt directly from Treasury. posts.text:
A good lesson in AI is that you need to check back in on the latest with every 3 to 6 months to try something that wasn’t possible before and see if it works again.

At no point in AI’s history is that more true than today. Just the past six months of model progress around computer and tool use, less context rot, better reasoning, multimodality, and deeper domain expertise in a number of key fields, these models are vastly more capable on what they can execute.

This is opening up a new vector of what AI systems will be able to autonomously work on. Essentially, anything with an API (and even many things without), we can anticipate that an agent will be able to control and utilize as an underlying capability to complete a process.

This means that we are no longer dependent on *just* the models generating everything from whole cloth, but instead they can fully utilize existing systems (or new ones purpose built for them) very effectively. This creates immense leverage for agents.

Security agents can leverage existing data feeds and cyber tooling, IT agents that can execute workflows reliably across software stacks, data agents that can migrate data or processes between systems, architect and design agents can leverage CAD and design tools, and on and on. And any of today’s tools that don’t work will likely be replaced by agent-friendly or OSS tooling that does the same. 

When you combine this with the domain understanding being trained into agents, you started to get autonomous collaborators for every job function and industry. This will open up a ton of new opportunities in AI if you build with this understanding in mind.

posts.name: Patrick Collison
posts.text:
Two things I’ve been thinking about regarding AI:

• People often highlight the risks involved in AI, which are surely very real. I’m struck, however, by how hard it is to understand the contours of the positive scenario. There are easy-to-perceive and frequently invoked elements of a positive vision — more diseases cured, more material abundance, etc. — which sound great, but these are by themselves just ingredients. I’m curious what the larger equilibrium is supposed to look like. Do people work? If so, why? What is their marginal contribution? If not, how are resources allocated? What is scarce? What is the ratio between humans and AIs? Are humans in control, whatever that means? One sometimes hears the Culture novels invoked as one scenario, but I’m not sure they depict a desirable outcome. (AI runs everything and humans compete in games? Iain Banks himself said that the humans in the Culture are “somewhere between passengers, pets and parasites.”) There is Richard Brautigan’s famous poem, but do we want to be “returned to our mammal brothers and sisters”? (Isn’t that rewinding Genesis?) We could say that it was hard to imagine the world of 1900 from the vantage point of 1700, and that’s assuredly true. But nobody in 1700 was trying to recast humanity itself within a couple of years — things necessarily unfolded slowly and by increments, and therefore with the possibility for error correction. Given how rapid the rate of progress in AI may be, it feels strange for the upside case to be so opaque.

• There is increasing discussion of whether AIs are conscious or how we would know whether they are, with conclusions there often assumed to be relevant to matters of moral worth. At first blush, this seems a rather arcane, benign, or even absurd issue. (Remember the response to Blake Lemoine’s fears.) Setting aside the terms of the debate itself, or the relevant demarcation criteria, it seems to me a quite high-stakes question, for an affirmative answer — that is, granting moral worth to AIs — would presumably mean that the aggregate worth of AIs would soon outweigh that of humans in any utilitarian calculus. The AIs will be exceptionally wise and intelligent, and vastly more numerous (especially once one considers the imminent future and the AIs not yet born). As such, even epsilon of moral worth will multiply to a lot once one considers the quadrillions that could soon exist. (This is effectively a distributed version of the Nozick’s utility monster.) If this conclusion is unpalatable, I think one of three propositions needs to be rejected: the premise AIs can have moral worth; utilitarianism itself; or the belief that there is even a possibility that they will be far more numerous than humans.

With both of these matters (contours of future society; AI moral worth), there is the possibility of dramatic change. Today, people argue about datacenters. I’m curious how popular support for AI will evolve as more people come to understand these medium-term questions and the relevant stakes. What is the vision for AI that most people would be excited about?

quoted.text:
当全世界的聪明人都在为近 4 万亿美元市值灰飞烟灭捶胸顿足时，硅谷风投大佬 Chamath 却掏出放大镜，找到了一个真正决定 AI 巨头生死的命门。

这位硅谷老狐狸抛出了一个暴论：眼下整场 AI 博弈的胜负，全看一单买卖。他指的，正是马斯克的 SpaceX 和 Anthropic 签下的那份算力合同，里面藏着一个“双向 90 天随时解约”的条款。

这事还得从这周的政治海啸说起。美国中期选举共和党遭遇了水门事件以来最惨的溃败，连红了几十年的德州都翻蓝了。州长们听见“数据中心”四个字就像见了瘟神，因为选民们早就受够了：这些庞大的机房除了替科技巨头赚钱，留给当地人的只有昂贵的水电费和噪音。

各地要是真给新数据中心按下暂停键，算力供给立马就得卡脖子。

就在这个节骨眼，硅谷的阶级成分瞬间清晰了。手里有现成地盘和电力的微软、谷歌、Meta、亚马逊，外加马斯克的 SpaceX，成了紧俏的“房东”；而像 Anthropic 和 OpenAI 这种得急需算力来迭代大模型的实验室，说白了，只是群没有房产证的“租客”。

在 Chamath 看来，这直接把马斯克送上了牌桌的主位。

手握着庞大算力，一旦数据中心审批放缓导致算力紧缺，现货价格可能会翻倍甚至涨到三倍。如果现货暴涨让原有长约变成了亏本买卖，SpaceX 随时可能直接动用“提前 90 天解约”的条款撕毁老合同，把算力按现货价重新计价。

到那时候，急需算力续命的 Anthropic 除了当场滑跪、认下翻倍甚至三倍的高价，根本没有第二条路可走。

就在这两天的富达路演上，面对机构把 IPO 估值从 2 万亿美元狠砍到 1.2 万亿的“骨折价”，CEO 达里奥为了保住上市，硬是诚恳地向买方投资者连说了三次“谢谢”。现在就开始赔笑脸了，真等到马斯克拔电源那天，他们更是连谈判的筹码都没有。

更损的是，这一刀要是真捅下去，等于当场给其他“房东”上了一堂生动的现实主义扫盲课，启发它们重新盘算手里的算力到底是留给自己用，还是拿去放高价租。而那些“二房东”们，为了不被踢出局，只能咬碎后槽牙，不计代价地去抢购市面上残存的算力。

听到这儿，旁边的 Jason 赶紧踩了脚刹车。他反驳说，马斯克跟 OpenAI 的奥特曼确实仇深似海，但跟 Anthropic 团队的关系好得像蜜月期，而且 Anthropic 还是他未来搞太空数据中心的好搭档。就算现货涨上天，马斯克也未必会干出直接掀桌子按现货价宰客的事，大家坐下来谈个“中间价”才更像人话。

但 Chamath 显然不相信硅谷的塑料兄弟情：“这跟关系好不好无关，跟谁是好公司坏公司也无关。这就是一张算账的表格，表格会直接给出答案。”

在这场近 4 万亿美元灰飞烟灭的魔幻风暴里，所谓的科技宏大叙事，剥开来看依然是最朴素的包租公哲学：只要电表转得够快、现货涨得够狠，再美好的革命友谊，可能也熬不过一张 Excel 表格，和一纸短短 90 天的逐客令。

3. Optimizing for ETH as SoV is aligned with decentralization and CROPS

Whenever I ask what people appreciate the most about Ethereum (as opposed to either other blockchains, or anything outside the blockchain world), the most common answer is: decentralization and CROPS (censorship and capture resistance, open source, privacy and security).

Decentralization and CROPS have a lot of value, even to institutions. For individuals, privacy is often viewed as an abstract ideology. For institutions, it's prudent risk management, data protection law compliance, and a number of other things. Likewise for security. And likewise for running your own node (enterprise buzzword: "on-prem deployment").

But what about for the ETH holder? Well, it depends why you're an ETH holder. If you want ETH to optimally chase financial trends and collect fees from them, then you want a Fearless Leader™ who bravely shouts on the socials that Ethereum loves [insert opportunity here] and will pragmatically reconfigure itself to give it explicit protocol support.

But if your primary reason to hold ETH is as an SoV, then you will be judging ETH by SoV-ish metrics. And what is the first and most important SoV-ish metric?

To survive.

That's what a big chunk of this last Devcon was about ("post-quantum and post-AI"). You want a chain that is taking conservative tradeoffs ("hash-only security, all formally proven, >3x more rounds than known to be necessary for security"). You want a chain that is aiming for at least partial ossification, where the great balance of work will move to higher levels of the stack once the core is complete. You want a chain that aims to minimize protocol politics, by having a very high bar before it accepts either precompiles that bloat the protocol or new kinds of in-protocol rewards that could get captured.

What other SoV'ish metrics?

The ability to easily hold it safely (hence, work on multisigs).
The ability to hold it privately (hence, kohaku work).
The ability to hold it privately *and* safely (hence, 8288 and private-AA workstreams already starting).
The guarantee that if you have coins, you can send them, and block builders can't stop you (FOCIL)
Minimized infrastructure dependence (basically the whole decentralization roadmap, including the fact that I am able to currently run a node on this laptop, and it synced in < 6 hours and takes up only 1/8 of my hard drive - better stats than in 2019!)

Now, are there "adoption" goals that are highly synergistic with SoV?

Very much so.

The more assets there are natively issued on L1, including both RWAs and native decentralized assets, the larger a set of things you can "do" with your ETH, the better. Being able to easily (including safely, trustlessly) convert back and forth between ETH and other assets, use ETH as collateral to do things with other assets, etc, all forms part of the utility of holding ETH.

There are still some conflicts between serving these use cases and decentralization (eg. we want to be careful about fast slots and impact on centralization), but on the whole much less than what you get if you maximize fees.

Conclusion:

The best social reason to care about Ethereum is because it makes decentralization and CROPS properties a reality for more people and uses.

The best private reason to hold ETH is its SoV properties, which are a direct consequence of that decentralization and CROPS.

2. Optimizing for ETH as fee-burning token would demand compromising decentralization and capture resistance

If we decide we actually want to optimize ETH for burning fees to justify a present-day ~$270B market cap, then Ethereum would essentially be functioning as a world-scale major corporation - it would be somewhere around L'Oreal (#55).

Now, what do *real* major corporations have to do in order to maintain their positions in the long term?

1. They spend. AI estimates L'Oreal as spending ~0.58% of its market cap per year on R&D. This would bankrupt the EF almost immediately. So this would require in-protocol funding to the tune of ~700k ETH per year, with all the political issues that it entails (so validator revenue would get cut by 2/3). And that's just R&D. Corporations have to spend on all kinds of things beyond just cranking out more units of their pre-existing product.
2. They govern. To survive new waves of technology and culture, you have to make highly opinionated choices to go after new markets, make new kinds of products with new features to appeal to people who think in new ways and use the newest technologies. Ethereum would need to have highly interventionist governance, for the long term.

Needless to say, both of these are far from conducive to optimizing capture resistance and decentralization.

On top of this there is another concern: optimizing for fee burning means optimizing for high gas prices to some degree. This may price out users, including some users who may need privacy and security the most. The price that maximizes price * usage leads to less usage than the price that allows as much usage as possible subject to safe blockchain resource limits.

I think what's being discussed here is whether funding stress in equity markets was a cause of leveraged unwinds.  Funding stress in equities CAN be a cause. Funding stress in equities CAN be within equities OR can be symptomatic of broad funding stress.  

Funding stress can be due to banks reaching narrow product leverage limits or broader leverage limits. OR can be caused by banks deleveraging for multiple reasons.  Funding stress can also occur when an end leverage investor in an already tight funding market (near limits) wants or needs to leverage up to hold positions. 

BUT as to recent equity selloff it was in no way caused by equity funding stress or broader leverage limits funding stress and was entirely due to the thing that was levered moving a lot more than expected.  The unwind actually reduces funding stress as the lender gets repaid
